blocks.text: I can describe the physical and chemical properties and some uses of transition metals, and compare them to Group 1 metals.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: A metal element placed in the block between Groups 2 and 3 in the periodic table.
A chemical that speeds up the rate of a reaction without itself being used up.
An atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge due to the loss or gain of electrons.
Calculated by dividing the mass of a substance by its volume; a measurement of how tightly packed a substance’s particles are per unit volume.

blocks.text: Transition metals are found in the {centre} of the periodic table, between Groups 2 and 3.
This block contains most of the metals on the periodic table, including familiar ones like silver, gold, iron and copper.
It helps to keep a periodic table to hand and get to know some of the symbols.
Transition metals have the typical physical properties of metals. Tap the three tricky words.

items.def: Can be bent or hammered into shape without shattering.
Can be drawn out into long wires without snapping or breaking.
Makes a ringing sound when you tap it.

items: good conductors of heat and electricity
high melting and boiling points (other than mercury)

blocks.text: Mercury is the exception: it is a liquid at room temperature. Its melting point is −39 °C.
Some transition metals are {magnetic}.
Uses that rely on magnetic metals:

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: Not all transition metals are magnetic. Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic, but it is not a property of every transition metal.
Transition metals are generally **stronger**, **harder** and **denser** than Group 1 metals, and they have **higher melting points**.

blocks.label: How much higher?
blocks.text: Iron melts at 1538 °C and potassium at 63.5 °C. 1538 − 63.5 = 1474.5, so iron’s melting point is 1474.5 °C higher.

blocks.label: Worked example: density
blocks.text: Density = mass ÷ volume. A piece of metal has a mass of 78.7 g and a volume of 10 cm³. Density = 78.7 ÷ 10 = 7.87 g/cm³, which is the density of iron.
Their strength and other physical properties make transition metals useful in construction and manufacturing.

blocks.q: Is each statement about Group 1 metals (like potassium) or transition metals?

items.text: Very soft: can be cut with a scalpel

items.q: Which of these is used in electrical wiring?
Manganese is added to steel to improve its …
Which of these is one of the magnetic metals named in this lesson?

blocks.text: Transition metals can form ions with different charges. This is because their atoms can lose different numbers of electrons.
Iron can form both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions. The iron atom either gives away two electrons or three electrons.

items.title: compounds with {Fe³⁺}
items.sub: orange-brown (iron hydroxide) or red-brown (iron oxide, rust)

blocks.text: How many electrons the metal loses changes the properties of its compounds, including their colour.
Transition metals are known for forming coloured compounds and solutions. Many paints and pigments contain transition metal compounds.
Most other metals form white compounds, which become colourless when dissolved in water. Sodium chloride solution is colourless.
The same metal ion can give different colours depending on the other ions present: copper sulfate (CuSO₄) is blue but copper oxide (CuO) is black.

blocks.q: Match each ion to the colour of its compounds.

blocks.text: Because a transition metal can form more than one ion, we put a Roman numeral in its name to show the charge. Chromium(II) means Cr²⁺ and chromium(III) means Cr³⁺.
The charges in a compound must balance so that the compound is neutral overall. Look at the two iron families:
That is why the Roman numerals matter: iron(II) and iron(III) make different compounds.
Step 1: use the Roman numeral to find the metal ion. Step 2: balance the charges. Tap each row.

rows.note: copper(II) sulfate: the charges are equal and opposite, so you need one of each.
nickel(II) nitrate: nitrate is 1−, so you need two nitrate ions for one nickel ion. Put the nitrate in brackets with a subscript 2.
chromium(III) oxide: two 3+ ions (6+) balance three 2− oxide ions (6−).
manganese(IV) oxide: the manganese ion is 4+, and oxide is 2−, so you need two oxide ions per manganese ion.

items.q: Copper(II) chloride contains Cu²⁺ ions and chloride ions (Cl⁻). What is its formula?
Chromium(III) chloride contains Cr³⁺ ions and chloride ions (Cl⁻). What is its formula?
In Fe₂O₃ each oxide ion is O²⁻. What is the charge on each iron ion?
What is the name of Fe(NO₃)₃?

blocks.text: Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals react slowly with water or do not react at all.

items.title: With {water}
items.sub: Group 1: vigorous, forming hydroxides and hydrogen gas. Transition metals: slow or none (more reactive with steam).

items.title: With {oxygen}
items.sub: Group 1: form oxides when left in air. Transition metals: form oxides when heated (metal powder burns).

items.title: With {halogens}
items.sub: Group 1: vigorous. Transition metals: less vigorous. Both form metal halides.

items.q: A piece of iron is put into cold water. What is most likely to happen?
options: It reacts slowly or not at all
It reacts vigorously and gives off hydrogen
is used up in the reaction
speeds up a reaction without being used up

blocks.text: Many transition metals are widely used as {catalysts} in industrial processes.

items.title: chromium
items.sub: making polymers used in packaging and containers

items.title: iron
items.sub: turning nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia (Haber process)

items.title: cobalt
items.sub: turning hydrogen and carbon monoxide into liquid fuels and waxes

items.title: copper
items.sub: turning hydrogen, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide into methanol

blocks.text: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down slowly into water and oxygen: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). A catalyst speeds this up. Comparing four metal oxides, manganese(IV) oxide made a large number of bubbles very quickly, while zinc(II) oxide made very few and the reaction was very slow.

blocks.label: Fair testing idea
blocks.text: The best catalyst is the one that makes the most bubbles of oxygen. To improve the method, collect the gas in a gas syringe and measure the volume of gas in a set time (for example one minute), then calculate the reaction rate.

items: Transition metals are generally stronger, harder and denser than Group 1 metals, and have higher melting points.
Transition metals react slowly with water or don’t react with it at all.
Transition metals are often catalysts that speed up chemical reactions.
Transition metals can form ions with different charges, and their compounds often have vibrant colours.

flashcards.front: Where are the transition metals in the periodic table?
flashcards.back: In the centre block, between Groups 2 and 3.

flashcards.front: Transition metals compared with Group 1 metals: strength, hardness, density and melting point?
flashcards.back: Generally stronger, harder and denser, with higher melting points.
Iron, cobalt and nickel (but not all transition metals are magnetic).

flashcards.front: Which metal element is a liquid at room temperature?
flashcards.back: Mercury, the exception to the high melting points of transition metals. Its melting point is −39 °C.

flashcards.front: How do transition metals typically react with water?
flashcards.back: Slowly, or not at all (unlike Group 1 metals). They are more reactive with steam.

flashcards.front: Why can transition metals form ions with different charges?
flashcards.back:
Their atoms can lose different numbers of electrons.

Iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.

flashcards.front: What colour are compounds containing Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺?
flashcards.back:
Fe²⁺: pale green.
Fe³⁺: orange-brown (or red-brown, as in rust).

flashcards.front: What do Roman numerals in a name like chromium(III) show?
flashcards.back: The charge on the metal ion: chromium(III) is Cr³⁺.

flashcards.front: What colour are most compounds of metals that are not transition metals?
flashcards.back: White (and colourless when dissolved in water).
A chemical that speeds up the rate of a reaction without itself being used up.

flashcards.front: Which transition metal is the catalyst in the Haber process?
flashcards.back: Iron (turning nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia).

flashcards.front: What is the formula for copper(II) sulfate?
flashcards.back:
CuSO₄

Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ have equal and opposite charges, so one of each.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Transition metals
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a word or a number.

questions.prompt: Which of these transition metals is used in electrical wiring: chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel or copper?
questions.explanation: Copper is a good conductor of electricity and is used in electrical wiring.

questions.prompt: Transition metals react ______ with water, or not at all. Fill in the gap with one word.
questions.explanation: Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals react slowly with water or not at all.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and which gas?
A piece of metal has a mass of 78.7 g and a volume of 10 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³? Give just the number.
Iron melts at 1538 °C and potassium melts at 63.5 °C. How many °C higher is the melting point of iron? Give just the number.
An iron atom loses electrons to form an Fe³⁺ ion. How many electrons does it lose?
questions.explanation: A 3+ ion is formed when an atom loses three electrons.

questions.prompt: What colour are compounds containing manganese(II) ions?
questions.explanation: Compounds containing Mn²⁺ ions are pink.

questions.prompt: How many nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) are needed for one nickel(II) ion (Ni²⁺) in nickel(II) nitrate? Give a number.
questions.explanation: Nickel(II) is 2+ and nitrate is 1−, so two nitrate ions balance one nickel ion: Ni(NO₃)₂.

questions.prompt: How many oxide ions (O²⁻) balance two chromium(III) ions (Cr³⁺) in chromium(III) oxide? Give a number.
questions.explanation: Two 3+ ions give 6+, and three 2− ions give 6−, so the formula is Cr₂O₃.

questions.prompt: Which word describes a chemical that speeds up a reaction without being used up?
questions.explanation: That is the meaning of catalyst.
